[[Category:Glasgow Name Study]]

== Biography ==
'''Hugh de Glasgw''' witnessed a lay quitclaim concerning three perticates of land in Glasgow's Rottenrow. The act is assigned to about 1283 rather than internally dated.<ref>''Registrum Monasterii de Passelet'', no. 341; [https://deeds.utsc.utoronto.ca/charters/06190339 DEEDS 06190339].</ref>

The same 1283 property dossier separately identifies [[Space:Alexander_son_of_Richard_messenger_of_Glasgow|Alexander, son of the late Richard the messenger of Glasgow]] and [[Space:Alexander_son_of_Richard_constable_of_Glasgow|Alexander, son of Richard the former constable of Glasgow]].<ref>''Registrum Monasterii de Passelet'', pp. 383–385; [https://deeds.utsc.utoronto.ca/charters/06190338/ DEEDS 06190338] and [https://deeds.utsc.utoronto.ca/charters/06190340/ DEEDS 06190340].</ref> They are associated people in a compact burgage network, not proved relatives of Hugh or proved hereditary Glasgow bearers.

Because the instrument already identifies Glasgow as the venue yet still distinguishes Hugh personally as `de Glasgw`, the phrase has strong personal-byname function. The source does not call him a burgess, landholder, neighbour or officeholder.

== Research Notes ==
The text survives through the later Paisley cartulary, not an autograph thirteenth-century instrument. No family relationship to another bearer is stated. Hugh's deed also identifies Peter de Castro as son of the deceased Alexander de Castro; that relationship belongs to the de Castro family and supplies no parentage for Hugh or either Alexander son of Richard.
